Bug: ColumnType.DecimalSize panics with nil deref when wrapper has nil SQLColumnType (driver returns partially-populated wrappers under concurrent DROP COLUMN)

## GORM Playground Link

https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/850

## Description

`migrator.ColumnType` is a wrapper struct with a named field `SQLColumnType *sql.ColumnType`. Several wrapper methods (`DecimalSize`, `Length`, `Nullable`, `ScanType`, and the SQLColumnType branches of `Name`/`DatabaseTypeName`) delegate to that field without checking whether it is `nil`. When a driver populates the wrapper from one source (e.g. `information_schema.columns`) but does not attach the `*sql.ColumnType` from a follow-up `SELECT * FROM <table> LIMIT 1` — because the column-name match between the two queries fails — the returned wrapper has `SQLColumnType == nil`. The next caller (typically `MigrateColumn`) panics on the first delegating method call.

A guard like `if columnType == nil` at the call site does NOT protect: the wrapper is a non-nil value type, and the nil pointer is the named field, not the wrapper itself.

### Source location

Wrapper struct: https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/blob/v1.31.1/migrator/column_type.go#L8-L24

```go
type ColumnType struct {
    SQLColumnType    *sql.ColumnType
    NameValue        sql.NullString
    DataTypeValue    sql.NullString
    ColumnTypeValue  sql.NullString
    ...
}
```

Vulnerable methods (delegate to `ct.SQLColumnType.X()` without a nil check):

```go
// migrator/column_type.go:71-76
func (ct ColumnType) DecimalSize() (precision int64, scale int64, ok bool) {
    if ct.DecimalSizeValue.Valid {
        return ct.DecimalSizeValue.Int64, ct.ScaleValue.Int64, true
    }
    return ct.SQLColumnType.DecimalSize()  // <-- panics if SQLColumnType is nil
}

// Same shape at: Length (L63-68), Nullable (L79-84), ScanType (L92-97),
// and the delegating branches of Name (L27-32) and DatabaseTypeName (L40-45).
```

First observed call site: https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/blob/v1.31.1/migrator/migrator.go#L528

### How a driver ends up returning a nil-internal wrapper

The postgres driver builds wrappers in two passes inside [`(Migrator).ColumnTypes`](https://github.com/go-gorm/postgres/blob/v1.6.0/migrator.go#L465-L540):

1. **Pass 1** — populate metadata from `information_schema.columns` into one wrapper per column the catalog reports.
2. **Pass 2** — execute `SELECT * FROM <table> LIMIT 1`, call `rows.ColumnTypes()`, then walk both lists and assign each `*sql.ColumnType` into the matching wrapper's `SQLColumnType` field ([driver/migrator.go:528-538](https://github.com/go-gorm/postgres/blob/v1.6.0/migrator.go#L528-L538)):

   ```go
   for _, columnType := range columnTypes {       // wrappers from pass 1
       for _, c := range rawColumnTypes {         // *sql.ColumnType from pass 2
           if c.Name() == columnType.Name() {
               columnType.(*migrator.ColumnType).SQLColumnType = c
               break
           }
       }
   }
   ```

If the `SELECT` itself errors, the function returns the error and no wrappers escape. The wrapper-with-nil-internal case happens when the `SELECT` **succeeds** but `rawColumnTypes` lacks a column the first pass surfaced — exactly the state produced by a concurrent `DROP COLUMN` between the two passes: `information_schema` (first pass) still observes the column under PostgreSQL's MVCC snapshot, but `SELECT * FROM <table>` (second pass) is issued against the post-DROP state. The wrapper for the dropped column survives with `SQLColumnType == nil`. The first method on it that delegates to `ct.SQLColumnType.X()` panics.

(The opposite race — `ADD COLUMN` between passes — is harmless: the new column simply has no wrapper at all.)

### Reproduction

Playground: https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/850 — `TestBug_DecimalSizeNilDerefOnRace` runs 50 race iterations of `AutoMigrate(&Supplier{})` against concurrent `DROP COLUMN`. Hit rate observed: ~30-40 panics per 50 iterations on a single

Question: Is the DEFAULT value the final determination of whether to alter a Column correct?

## Your Question

Why does the default value on a column being the same between the database and the struct prevent an alter being generated for a column?  (For SQLite it's a drop/recreate that should be done)

For example a struct with:
```TextColumn string `gorm:"type:bytes;size:255;index;default:'';"```
Against an SQLite database with 
```text_column TEXT NOT NULL COLLATE BINARY DEFAULT ''```
Will not generate an alter statement because the default: statement below results in false.
Note the difference between Bool and default vs Time and String.
https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/blob/0011f39aec713e282af1107d5561fd9d4b125fa8/migrator/migrator.go#L554-L569

Bool and default allow the DEFAULT being the same to change a column from being altered to not being altered.
Time and String will mark a column for altering, but NOT remove a column from being altered.

## The document you expected this should be explained

https://gorm.io/docs/migration.html#Auto-Migration


## Expected answer

If this is working as designed (ie. the DEFAULT on a column is the decider on whether it is altered), then it should be documented as so.

Bug : utils.FileWithLineNum returns inaccurate location after slog CallerFrame change

## GORM Playground Link

https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/845

## Description

As noted in https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/pull/7610#issuecomment-3877337170, after https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/pull/7610 was merged, a new regression was introduced.

Specifically, comparing v1.31.1 and v1.31.0 shows that the behavior of `utils.FileWithLineNum()` is inconsistent.

Here is a minimal reproduction:

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"os"
	"time"

	"gorm.io/gorm/logger"
	"gorm.io/gorm/utils"
)

func main() {
	demoExternal()
	demoSlog()
}

func where() string {
	return utils.FileWithLineNum() // line 20
}

func demoExternal() {
	actual := where() // line 24
	fmt.Println("external FileWithLineNum:", actual)
}

func demoSlog() {
	handler := slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stdout, &slog.HandlerOptions{AddSource: true})
	l := logger.NewSlogLogger(slog.New(handler), logger.Config{LogLevel: logger.Info})
	l.Trace(context.Background(), time.Now(), func() (string, int64) {
		return "select 1", 0
	}, nil)
}
```

`go.mod` with v1.31.0:

```
module hello

go 1.25.4

require gorm.io/gorm v1.31.0
```

Output:

```
external FileWithLineNum: /Users/nx/GolandProjects/hello/main.go:24
time=2026-02-28T00:43:55.136+08:00 level=INFO source=/Users/nx/go/pkg/mod/gorm.io/gorm@v1.31.0/logger/slog.go:87 msg="SQL executed" trace.duration=0.024ms trace.sql="select 1" trace.rows=0
```

But if we switch to v1.31.1:

```
module hello

go 1.25.4

require gorm.io/gorm v1.31.1
```

Output becomes:

```
external FileWithLineNum: /Users/nx/GolandProjects/hello/main.go:20 # this changed
time=2026-02-28T00:46:05.436+08:00 level=INFO source=/Users/nx/GolandProjects/hello/main.go:31 msg="SQL executed" trace.duration=0.017ms trace.sql="select 1" trace.rows=0
```

Please assign this issue to me; I am preparing a PR.  
This likely requires more than just changing a single number, and I will review related areas for other potential issues.

N+1 Queries with Joins("Company").Preload("Company.Addresses") on Addresses

## GORM Playground Link

https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/722

## Version 
Superior to v1.25.6

## Description
This issues to demonstrate an issue in GORM's query behavior. 

The function illustrates potential inefficiencies and unexpected results that may have been introduced due to a previous fix in GORM's preloading and join operations.

### Background
Previously, a [fix was implemented in GORM to address an issue where, when joining on Account.Pet and then preloading Account.Companies, the account was loaded twice](https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/issues/6715), even though it was already present in the main query. This fix aimed to improve the consistency and efficiency of the query process.

### Current Issue
However, the provided playground suggests that the fix may have unintentionally introduced another issue. The test highlights the following:

Unexpected Queries: The function is expected to execute two queries (one for fetching user data and another for related data). Instead, there may be an additional, unnecessary query, suggesting an n+1 query problem.

TLDR: 

```go
DB.Joins("Company").Preload("Company.Addresses").Find(&result).Error
```

is resulting in 

```
2024/04/23 15:08:19 /Users/alexisviscogliosi/dev/go-playground/db.go:59
[1.205ms] [rows:2] SELECT * FROM "addresses" WHERE "addresses"."company_id" = 1

2024/04/23 15:08:19 /Users/alexisviscogliosi/dev/go-playground/db.go:59
[0.634ms] [rows:2] SELECT * FROM "addresses" WHERE "addresses"."company_id" = 2

2024/04/23 15:08:19 /Users/alexisviscogliosi/dev/go-playground/db.go:59
[3.667ms] [rows:2] SELECT "users"."id","users"."created_at","users"."updated_at","users"."deleted_at","users"."name","Company"."id" AS "Company__id","Company"."name" AS "Company__name","Company"."user_id" AS "Company__user_id" FROM "users" LEFT JOIN "companies" "Company" ON "users"."id" = "Company"."user_id
```
_Note: if there is more than 2 companies it results in N queries where N is the number of companies._ 

Instead of 

```
SELECT `users`.`id`,`users`.`created_at`,`users`.`updated_at`,`users`.`deleted_at`,`users`.`name`,`Company`.`id` AS `Company__id`,`Company`.`name` AS `Company__name`,`Company`.`user_id` AS `Company__user_id` FROM `users
		LEFT JOIN `companies` `Company` ON `users`.`id` = `Company`.`user_id`
		WHERE `users`.`deleted_at` IS NULL
SELECT * FROM `companies` WHERE `companies`.`id` IN (1, 2)
```


In version v1.25.6 the select of addresses where using a IN clause but have the problem of doing a second query with companies (https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/issues/6715#issuecomment-1832455676)

db.Not method when used with multiple Where conditions has changed unexpectedly 

## GORM Playground Link

- https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/695
- https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/696

## Description

A regression introduced in Gorm v1.25.6, specifically in commit https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/commit/940358e0ddd1e6d5e893184943a4fa71a0c28521.

The behavior of the db.Not method when used with multiple Where conditions has changed unexpectedly. Prior to v1.25.6, the query `db.Not(db.Where("a=1").Where("b=1"))` would correctly translate to SQL as `NOT (a=1 AND b=1)`. However, after the specified commit, the same query started translating to `(NOT a=1 AND NOT b=1)`, which is a significant alteration in the logic.

I created PR (https://github.com/go-gorm/gorm/pull/6844) to address this issue.

Allowing Customization of Type and ID Column Names for Polymorphic associations

## Describe the feature

Allow users to customize the naming conventions for type and id columns when working with polymorphic associations in GORM, specifically for types specified using the `gorm:"polymorphic"` tag.



## Motivation

In scenarios where GORM is integrated with a database migrated by another language or framework, the default naming conventions for type and id columns may not align with the existing database schema. The need for customization becomes apparent, especially for types specified using the `gorm:"polymorphic"` tag.

The current GORM implementation assumes standard names (`<type>_id` and `<type>_type`), making it challenging to seamlessly integrate with databases where these conventions differ. To address this, there is a proposal to enhance GORM, allowing individual users to specify custom type and id column names for any type marked with the `gorm:"polymorphic"` tag. This enhancement ensures that GORM can adapt to diverse database schemas without risking compatibility issues.

Embedded nil pointer structs should be retrieved as nil

## Describe the feature

Gorm should round trip an embedded pointer to a struct as nil when the struct is given as nil.

## Motivation

My domain model has optional embedded objects, which then may have required fields on them.

Our validator will validate the embedded object's required fields if the pointer value is non-nil but will ignore the required validations on the embedded struct if it is nil.

Gorm should detect that that the embedded struct has the zero value and not set it to the zero value if only zero values have been loaded into that value.

Without this a save of nil is not preserved on reload for the embedded struct.

## Related Issues

- None that I could find.

@@ -90,9 +90,15 @@ func TestEmbeddedPointerTypeStruct(t *testing.T) {

## GORM Playground Link

## To Reproduce

Run the following query (includes the line-endings)
```sql
SELECT * FROM table
WHERE name1 = @name1
 AND name2 = @name2
```

## Description

If a named variable is followed by Windows CRLF style line endings, the variable name will include the `\r` portion of the line ending which causes the variable lookup in the `namedMap` to fail. In my PR, I've updated the expression builder to look for `\r` in addition to `\n`.

## Workaround
Put a space after the named variable so that there's a separator from this list of supported separators between the named variable and the CRLF line ending.

`FindInBatches` in an unexpected manner with `limit` or `offset` in original query

## GORM Playground Link



It's a reversed test, which means the CI SHOULD FAIL instead of success.

https://github.com/go-gorm/playground/pull/466

## Description



The use case is pretty simple. Consider we may have 1k user records, and we want to pre-filter 500 records by like, last login time, then process them in 5 per 100 records batch. The query use `FindInBatches` will be like:

```go
var singleBatch []User
dbInstance.Limit(500).Offset(100).Where("").FindInBatches(&singleBatch, 100, func(tx *gorm.DB, batch int) error {
  // Some operations over singleBatch
})
```

When using the `Limit` and `Offset` clauses, due to the implementation of `.FindInBatches`, it will cause different issues(Both are covered in the playground):
- `Limit`: The inner `Limit` by `.FindInBatches` will overwrite the originial query, which will fetch all records instead of the desired set.
- `Offset`: The parameter will be applied in each query, which will skip certain entries over the desired results.

By design, it leads to two solutions:

1. If it's the intended behavior, we may should add a *warning* section in the doc to tell the user not to use it with `limit` or `offset` clauses, or even refactor the API to avoid misusing.
2. If the pre-filtered query should be supported, we may need one or more queries overhead(s) to properly get the query sets since the `where` clause can be pretty complex and it's hard to handle them(e.g., a query will make the `id` or primary key field not continous).

}

}

  return "my_schema.table_two"
}
```

```
2022/01/26 17:14:17 /home/mnussbaum/go/pkg/mod/gorm.io/driver/postgres@v1.2.3/migrator.go:172 ERROR: syntax error at or near "." (SQLSTATE 42601)

NewFailoverClient panics with StreamingCredentialsProvider (nil streaming manager)

## Expected Behavior

A failover client created with `FailoverOptions.StreamingCredentialsProvider` authenticates new connections with the streaming provider, like `NewClient` does.

## Current Behavior

Every new connection panics in `initConn`:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
github.com/redis/go-redis/v9/internal/auth/streaming.(*Manager).Listener(0x0, ...)
	internal/auth/streaming/manager.go:107
	redis.go:982 (initConn)
```

`NewFailoverClient` passes `StreamingCredentialsProvider` to the client options (`sentinel.go`), but it never creates `streamingCredentialsManager`. Only `NewClient` creates it and registers its pool hook (`redis.go`, the `opt.StreamingCredentialsProvider != nil` block after the pipeline pool is built). `initConn` dereferences the manager whenever the provider is set.

This is the same class of bug as #4154 (fixed for `Conn()`/`EphemeralConn()`/`Tx` in #4155), but here it hits every connection, not only derived clients.

## Possible Solution

Move the manager setup from `NewClient` into a shared helper and call it from both constructors after the pipeline pool is built:

```go
// initStreamingCredentials creates the streaming-credentials manager and
// registers its pool hook on the main and pipeline pools.
func (c *baseClient) initStreamingCredentials() {
	if c.opt.StreamingCredentialsProvider == nil {
		return
	}
	workers := c.connPool.Size()
	if pp := c.getPipelinePool(); pp != nil {
		workers += pp.Size()
	}
	c.streamingCredentialsManager = streaming.NewManagerWithWorkers(c.connPool, c.opt.PoolTimeout, workers)
	c.connPool.AddPoolHook(c.streamingCredentialsManager.PoolHook())
	if pp := c.getPipelinePool(); pp != nil {
		pp.AddPoolHook(c.streamingCredentialsManager.PoolHook())
	}
}
```

cluster: ParseClusterURL TLS config has no MinVersion and pins the seed ServerName

## Problem

For `rediss://` URLs, `ParseClusterURL` builds the TLS config differently from the other URL parsers:

1. It does not set `MinVersion`. `ParseURL` (`options.go:972-974`) and `ParseFailoverURL` (`sentinel.go:440`) both set `MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12`. `ParseClusterURL` (`osscluster.go:374`) sets only `ServerName`, so a cluster client built from a URL accepts whatever minimum the Go `crypto/tls` default allows, not TLS 1.2.
2. `ServerName` is set to the seed host, and the same `*tls.Config` is passed to every node client (`osscluster.go:507`). Nodes discovered through `CLUSTER SLOTS`/`CLUSTER SHARDS` have other hostnames. Their certificates are therefore verified against the seed's name. This works only if every node certificate also covers the seed name, for example with a wildcard SAN.

## Repro

```go
opt, _ := redis.ParseClusterURL("rediss://user:pass@node-a.example:6379?addr=node-b.example:6379")
fmt.Println(opt.TLSConfig.MinVersion) // 0, ParseURL gives tls.VersionTLS12
fmt.Println(opt.TLSConfig.ServerName) // "node-a.example", also used when dialing node-b
```

## Expected

- The same `MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12` as `ParseURL` and `ParseFailoverURL`.
- Each node is verified against its own host. For example, leave `ServerName` empty in the parsed config so that `crypto/tls` uses the dialed host. Or clone the config per node and set `ServerName` from the node address when the user did not set one explicitly.

## Notes

- Both points come from reading the code on master; neither was reproduced against a TLS cluster.
- `skip_verify=true` (#4106) turns off all certificate checks. It should not become the usual workaround for point 2.
- #3475 (TLS URL parameters) touches the same block and should take this into account.

Found while reviewing #4106.

FailoverClient pub/sub dial has no timeout unless DialTimeout is set explicitly

## Expected Behavior

A failover client created without `DialTimeout` uses the 5 second default for every dial, as a single-server client does and as `client.Options().DialTimeout` reports.

## Current Behavior

The pub/sub dial of a failover client has no timeout of its own unless `FailoverOptions.DialTimeout` is set explicitly; only a deadline on the caller's context bounds it. When the master address drops packets (host powered off, network partition, firewall DROP), `Subscribe` blocks until the kernel gives up on the connect. On Linux with `net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries = 6` that took 133 to 136 seconds:

| Client | `Options().DialTimeout` | `Subscribe` returned after | Error |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NewClient`, default options | 5s | 5.0 s | `i/o timeout` |
| `NewFailoverClient`, `DialTimeout: 5 * time.Second` | 5s | 5.0 s | `i/o timeout` |
| `NewFailoverClient`, default options | 5s | 132.8 s, 135.9 s, 136.0 s | `connect: connection timed out` |

The table is from three runs on v9.22.0; the first two rows were 5.0 s in every run. One run each on v9.23.0-beta.1 and on master (f813adc) gave 133.2 s and 135.3 s for the last row, and 5.0 s for the first two.

## Possible Solution

From reading the code at v9.22.0. I have not tested a patch.

- `masterReplicaDialer` builds its dialer from the caller's `FailoverOptions`: `net.Dialer{Timeout: failover.opt.DialTimeout}` ([sentinel.go#L669-L672](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/sentinel.go#L669-L672)). An unset `DialTimeout` is still 0 there. The 5 second default is filled in by `opt.init()` on the `Options` copy that `clientOptions()` returns, which this dialer does not read.
- Pooled connections hide it: `ConnPool.dialConn` gives each attempt a context limited to `DialTimeout` ([internal/pool/pool.go#L721-L726](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/internal/pool/pool.go#L721-L726)). `PubSubPool.NewConn` passes the caller's context to the dialer as it is ([internal/pool/pubsub.go#L45](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/internal/pool/pubsub.go#L45)).
- `NewDialer`, used by a single-server client, reads `opt.DialTimeout` after `init()`, so it has the default.

Reading the timeout from the initialised client options in `masterReplicaDialer` would give both kinds of client the same bound. A URL parsed by `ParseFailoverURL` without `dial_timeout` leaves `DialTimeout` at 0 as well.

command: slice cmds stop at an error element and desync pipelines

Low priority. This is a hardening issue. No built-in command is known to trigger it on current Redis.

## Problem

`UintSliceCmd`, `FloatSliceCmd`, `StringSliceCmd` and `BoolSliceCmd` return from `readReply` at the first element that is a Redis error. The rest of the array stays unread. In a `Pipeline`/`TxPipeline`, `pipelineReadCmds` treats a Redis error as a reply that was read in full. The leftover elements are then read as the replies of the next commands, which get wrong values and no error.

#4071 (open) fixes this for `IntSliceCmd` only, because TS.MADD and CMS.INCRBY send error elements in the middle of the array.

## Repro

You can reach this with the public constructors through a custom command. Real wire, master 2821f880, Redis 8.10:

```go
pipe := rdb.Pipeline()
sc := redis.NewStringSliceCmd(ctx, "eval", "return {'a', redis.error_reply('boom'), 'c'}", 0)
_ = pipe.Process(ctx, sc)
echo := pipe.Echo(ctx, "next")
_, _ = pipe.Exec(ctx)
fmt.Printf("%q %v | %q %v\n", sc.Val(), sc.Err(), echo.Val(), echo.Err())
```

Reply bytes for each type (package-internal check):

```
*3\r\n$1\r\n1\r\n-ERR item failed\r\n$1\r\n1\r\n  then  $4\r\nnext\r\n
```

## Observed vs expected

```
P2 and P3: sc=["a" "" ""] err=ERR boom | ECHO "next" -> val="c" err=<nil>
```

The `ECHO` gets the third element of the `EVAL` reply. With the bytes above, all five types (`Int`, `Uint`, `Float`, `String`, `BoolSliceCmd`) return `ERR item failed`, and the next `ReadReply` returns `"1"` instead of `"next"`.

Expected: the cmd reads all elements, `Err()` is the first element error, and the next command reads `"next"`.

A single command outside a pipeline is mostly protected. `putConn` removes a connection that has unread buffered data ([internal/pool/pool.go:1489-1496](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/internal/pool/pool.go#L1489-L1496)). In the same run, an `ECHO` after a single `StringSliceCmd` read the correct reply. That check only sees bytes already in the bufio buffer, so a large or split reply can still get through.

## Evidence from real replies

I checked every built-in command that returns these types, on Redis 8.10 with RESP2 and RESP3. None sends an error element before the last one:

- `BoolSliceCmd`: BF.MADD and BF.INSERT on a full NONSCALING filter return `[1, 1, "ERR non scaling filter is full"]`. The error is always the last element, because the server truncates the array, so nothing is left unread. BF.MEXISTS, CF.MEXISTS, CF.INSERT (`-1` when full), TOPK.QUERY, SMISMEMBER and SCRIPT EXISTS return plain values or a top-level error.
- `FloatSliceCmd`: ZMSCORE, TDIGEST.QUANTILE/CDF/BYRANK/BYREVRANK return a top-level error on bad input.
- `StringSliceCmd`: JSON.ARRPOP `$..a` with a non-array match returns a nil element (`["2", nil]`), not an error. TOPK.ADD returns nil elements. TS.QUERYINDEX, FT._LIST, VSIM and VRANGE have no error elements.
- `UintSliceCmd`: ARGREP only.
- TS.MGET is not one of these types (`MapStringSliceInterfaceCmd`).

## Root cause

Each loop has `case err != nil: return err`:

- `UintSliceCmd.readReply`: [command.go:1656](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L1656)
- `FloatSliceCmd.readReply`: [command.go:2087](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L2087)
- `StringSliceCmd.readReply`: [command.go:2162](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L2162)
- `BoolSliceCmd.readReply`: [command.go:2429](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L2429)

The same pattern is at [command.go:2240](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L2240) (nested string slices), [5503](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2821f8801fb6b65c0db2537296ec164d3644290e/command.go#L5

Output from master 2821f880 against Redis 8.10:

P2 WITHSCORES EXPLAINSCORE           err=invalid field value format
   raw=[2 doc:2 [0.1219... [Final BM25 : ... [...]]] [t hello there] doc:1 [0.0927... [...]] [t hello world]]
P2 NOCONTENT WITHSCORES EXPLAINSCORE err=invalid document ID format
P2 RETURN 0                          err=invalid document fields format
   raw=[2 doc:2 doc:1]
P2 options=nil                       panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

P3 WITHSCORES EXPLAINSCORE           err=<nil> docs=[doc:2 score=nil ...; doc:1 score=nil ...]

options: URL dialer_retry_timeout <= 0 uses the default, and negative buffer sizes are accepted

## Problem

1. The `ParseURL` doc says (`options.go:911`): "to disable a duration field, use value less than or equal to 0". `dialer_retry_timeout` does not follow this. A value <= 0 parses to a negative duration, and the pool's dial retry backoff (`internal/pool/pool.go:788-791`) treats a non-positive value as the 100ms default. So `dialer_retry_timeout=0` or `=-1` gives the default 100ms delay between dial retries, not "disabled". `ParseClusterURL` and `ParseFailoverURL` already behaved this way, and #4063 adds the same option to `ParseURL`.
2. `read_buffer_size` and `write_buffer_size` accept negative values. `ReadBufferSize=-1` ends up as bufio's 16-byte minimum, the same as setting `-1` in Go. Neither the URL parser nor `Options.init` rejects it or maps it to the default.

## Repro

```go
opt, _ := redis.ParseClusterURL("redis://localhost:6379?dialer_retry_timeout=-1&read_buffer_size=-1")
fmt.Println(opt.DialerRetryTimeout, opt.ReadBufferSize) // -1ns -1
// The pool waits 100ms between dial retries, and reads use a 16-byte buffer.
```

## Suggested fix

- Choose one meaning for `DialerRetryTimeout <= 0` (default, or "no delay") and document it on the field. Then either make the URL doc rule hold for this field, or list it as an exception in the `ParseURL` doc.
- In `Options.init`, map negative buffer sizes to the default, or return an error from the URL parser for negative sizes.

Then `reAuthFn(context.DeadlineExceeded)` reaches `onAuthenticationErr`, `isBadConn` treats the deadline error as a bad connection, the connection is closed with

```
redis: re-authentication failed: context deadline exceeded
```

and the next command dials a replacement. While the connection is marked, `OnGet` rejects it on every checkout, so it serves nothing and holds its pool slot; with the pool at `PoolSize`, every command in that window dials and then drops a replacement.

Whenever the worker has enqueued itself before Put releases the connection, the waiter is never served; because the pool is LIFO, the connection then sits at the bottom of the idle stack and nothing transitions it again until the worker's context deadline. `TryTransitionFast`, which the comment on `Release()` points to, is a bare CAS as well. A second, narrower ordering also loses the wake-up: when `Release()` runs between the worker's failed fast path and its enqueue, there is no waiter to notify yet and the enqueue comes too late. Both orderings occur in the reproduction, and a change for either one alone leaves the other (measured below). Because the fast path is skipped whenever `waiterCount > 0`, a later `OnNext` for the same connection queues a second worker behind the stuck one and does not unstick it (verified: a second push of the same credentials fails at the same rate).

ClusterOptions: ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout -1 gives node clients the 5s default

## Expected Behavior

`ReadTimeout: -1` / `WriteTimeout: -1` on `ClusterOptions` means no timeout, same as on `Options`. Each node client should end up with a timeout of 0.

## Current Behavior

Node clients use the 5s default. `ClusterOptions.init` turns `-1` into `0`, and then `Options.init` on each node client turns that `0` into 5s. So any command that takes longer than 5s fails with an i/o timeout even with `-1`. The same happens through `UniversalOptions` when it builds a cluster client.

`-2` works on clusters. `Ring` and the failover client pass `-1` through untouched, so they work too.

## Possible Solution

Don't let the node clients see the already-normalized `0`. For example, map `0` back to `-1` when building the node options in `newClusterNodeWithNodeAddress`, so `Options.init` handles it like it does for a plain client.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a Redis server with `--enable-debug-command yes` (a single node is enough, using `ClusterSlots`).
2. Run:

```go
ctx := context.Background()
rdb := redis.NewClusterClient(&redis.ClusterOptions{
	ClusterSlots: func(ctx context.Context) ([]redis.ClusterSlot, error) {
		return []redis.ClusterSlot{{Start: 0, End: 16383, Nodes: []redis.ClusterNode{{Addr: "127.0.0.1:6379"}}}}, nil
	},
	ReadTimeout:  -1,
	WriteTimeout: -1,
})
_ = rdb.ForEachShard(ctx, func(ctx context.Context, shard *redis.Client) error {
	fmt.Println(shard.Options().ReadTimeout, shard.Options().WriteTimeout)
	return nil
})
fmt.Println(rdb.Do(ctx, "DEBUG", "SLEEP", "6").Err())
```

3. It prints `5s 5s`, then `read tcp ...: i/o timeout`.
4. With `redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{ReadTimeout: -1, ...})` the same command succeeds.

## Context (Environment)

go-redis master (9.23.0-beta.1), Go 1.27. Found while documenting the timeout options on `UniversalOptions` (#4045).

## Detailed Description

`ClusterOptions.init` normalizes the timeouts for the cluster's own pipeline and tx paths, but `clientOptions()` forwards the normalized values to `NewClient`, which normalizes them a second time. The mapping isn't idempotent for `-1`.

## Possible Implementation

I have a small fix with a unit test and will open a PR.

Document timeout semantics on UniversalOptions

`UniversalOptions` exposes the same timeout-related fields that eventually get passed into the concrete Redis client options, but their comments currently don't explain the behavior of those values.

In particular:

```go
ReadTimeout           time.Duration
WriteTimeout          time.Duration
ContextTimeoutEnabled bool
```

are much less documented than the corresponding fields on `Options`, where the timeout defaults and the special `-1` / `-2` values are described.

Since `UniversalOptions` is configured directly when using `NewUniversalClient`, it would be nice to have that information available on the type itself. Otherwise users reading the API in an IDE or on pkg.go.dev have to jump to another options type to understand what those values mean.

The semantics appear to be shared anyway, since the universal options are forwarded into the simple, cluster, or failover configuration.

This looks like it could be fixed by reusing or adapting the existing comments from the concrete options.

No runtime behavior needs to change - just bringing the public documentation for `UniversalOptions` in line with the options it maps to.

Native OpenTelemetry metrics count cache misses(`redis.Nil`) as internal client errors

## Expected Behavior

A `GET` for a key that does not exist returns `redis.Nil`. This is a successful command that returned an empty reply, so it should not be counted in `redis.client.errors` (`redis_client_errors_total`).

If nil replies are recorded for visibility, they should at least be distinguishable from real failures rather than being reported as unknown internal client errors.

## Current Behavior

With native OpenTelemetry(`extra/redisotel-native`) metrics enabled, every `redis.Nil` reply increments `redis.client.errors` metrics with:

```text
error.type = UNKNOWN
db.response.status_code = UNKNOWN
redis.client.errors.internal = true
redis.client.errors.category = server
```

## Possible Solution

The error path appears to invoke the metrics error callback for every non-nil error. Since `redis.Nil` is an error, it reaches error classification, matches no known case, and falls through to the `UNKNOWN` / `internal=true` catch-all.

Two options:

**1. Preferred — do not record `redis.Nil` as an error:**

Skip the metrics error callback when `errors.Is(err, redis.Nil)`, and apply the same guard to the error attributes on `db.client.operation.duration`.

If maintaining a datapoint for nil replies is preferred, classify them explicitly (for example `error.type="NIL"`, `internal=false`, `category="cache_miss"`) instead of relying on the `UNKNOWN` fallback.

**2. Alternative — give nil replies their own non-failure category:**

```text
error.type = NIL
db.response.status_code = NIL
redis.client.errors.internal = false
redis.client.errors.category = cache_miss
```

This keeps the datapoint but lets dashboards and alerts exclude cache misses from error rates and success-rate calculations.

## Steps to Reproduce

Minimal reproduction repository: https://github.com/leonardovillela/redis-otel-native-metrics-cache-miss-error-metrics-bug

1. Clone the repository and run `make`. This starts Redis, a Go reproducer, the OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus and Grafana via Docker Compose.
2. The reproducer enables native metrics before creating the client:

```go
instrumentation := redisotel.GetObservabilityInstance()
err := instrumentation.Init(
    redisotel.NewConfig().
        WithEnabled(true).
        WithMetricGroups(redisotel.MetricGroupAll),
)
```

3. It then issues 10 `GET` requests per second for a key that does not exist:

```go
client := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{Addr: "redis:6379"})

for range time.NewTicker(100 * time.Millisecond).C {
    err := client.Get(ctx, "missing-key").Err()
    if !errors.Is(err, redis.Nil) {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}
```

4. Open Grafana at http://localhost:3000 (`admin` / `admin`) and view the **Redis Client Observability Dashboard**. `redis.client.errors` increases by ~10/second with `error.type="UNKNOWN"` and `redis.client.errors.internal="true"`, even though every command returned the expected `redis.Nil`.

Run `make stop` to tear the stack down.

## Context (Environment)

A read-heavy service with a normal cache-miss rate reports a large, permanent client error rate and a degraded success rate. Because misses are classified as `UNKNOWN` internal errors, there is no way to separate them from genuine client failures, which makes error-rate dashboards, alerts and error budgets unusable without knowing this quirk.

- `github.com/redis/go-redis/v9`: `v9.22.0`
- `github.com/redis/go-redis/extra/redisotel-native/v9`: `v9.22.0`
- OpenTelemetry Go SDK: `v1.43.0`
- Go: `1.25`
- Redis server: Docker `redis:latest`

## Detailed Description

`redis.Nil` signals an empty reply, not a failed operation, but it is currently funnelled through the same classification path as real errors. Because it matches no known error case, it is reported as an unknown internal client error.

Cache misses are expected behavior for most Redis workloads, so counting them as errors conflates normal operation with failure.

Conn.Close skips socket cleanup after initConn transitions to StateClosed

### Description

When connection initialization fails, `baseClient.initConn` transitions the pool connection to `StateClosed` before returning the error. The pool then removes the rejected connection and calls `Conn.Close()`, but `Conn.Close()` immediately returns when it observes `StateClosed`.

That early return skips:

- the per-connection `onClose` callback (including streaming-credential unsubscribe),
- the CSC close callback, and
- `net.Conn.Close()`.

Repeated initialization/authentication failures can therefore accumulate open sockets/file descriptors until garbage collection.

This is present in v9.22.0 and remains present on current `master` (`216593cc01faa029006266a5f1fc3d5004312ecf`).

### Relevant paths

Initialization marks the connection closed before returning:

- [`redis.go` v9.22.0, `initConn`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/redis.go#L737-L780)
- Authentication and handshake failure paths do the same later in that function.

The rejected-connection path calls `CloseConn`, which ultimately calls `cn.Close()`:

- [`internal/pool/pool.go` v9.22.0](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/internal/pool/pool.go#L1584-L1600)
- [`internal/pool/pool.go` v9.22.0, `closeConn`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/internal/pool/pool.go#L1654-L1656)

`Conn.Close()` returns before resource cleanup if the state is already closed:

- [`internal/pool/conn.go` v9.22.0](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/v9.22.0/internal/pool/conn.go#L1111-L1139)

### Reproduction outline

1. Start a local TCP listener and count accepted/open connections.
2. Create a client using a `StreamingCredentialsProvider` whose subscription or authentication path fails after the socket has been dialed.
3. Repeatedly issue a command such as `PING`, without forcing GC.
4. Observe that each attempt is rejected and removed from the pool, but the corresponding server-side socket remains open and the process file-descriptor count grows.

A focused internal regression test can avoid timing/GC dependence by using a recording `net.Conn` and close callback:

1. Put the connection into the same initialized transport state as a newly dialed pool connection.
2. transition it to `StateClosed`, mirroring the `initConn` failure path;
3. invoke the pool removal/close path;
4. assert the underlying `net.Conn.Close()` and installed close callback each execute exactly once.

### Expected behavior

Resource cleanup should be idempotent and independent of whether the state machine has already transitioned to `StateClosed`. A rejected initialization should synchronously close the transport and run close callbacks exactly once.

### Actual behavior

`Conn.Close()` treats `StateClosed` as proof that cleanup already happened, although `initConn` uses that state to report failure before cleanup. It returns `nil` without closing the transport or callbacks.

### Possible direction

Track cleanup completion separately from logical connection state, or make `Close()` always atomically drain callbacks and close the transport even when the state is already `StateClosed`. A `sync.Once`/atomic-swap style cleanup would retain idempotence without conflating “marked closed” with “resources released.”

This may be related in theme to #3703, but the reproduction and leak point are different: this report concerns initialization/authentication failure before a connection becomes usable, rather than a closed connection remaining in `idleConns`.

RouteByLatency picks a strict minimum, so equally-close nodes get no read traffic

## Expected Behavior

With `RouteByLatency` enabled on a cluster or failover-cluster client, read-only commands
should be distributed across nodes that are effectively equidistant from the client, so a set
of replicas in the same locality shares the read load.

## Current Behavior

`clusterState.slotClosestNode` selects the strict minimum, with no tolerance band:

```go
for _, n := range nodes {
    if closestNode == nil || n.Latency() < minLatency {
        closestNode = n
        minLatency = n.Latency()
        ...
    }
}
```

Every client therefore converges on whichever node measured marginally lowest, and its
equally-close peers take no read traffic at all. The estimate driving that decision is coarse
— `updateLatency` takes the mean of ten `PING`s of a sub-millisecond operation, and the value
is refreshed at most every 10s (`minLatencyMeasurementInterval`) — so a difference well inside
the measurement noise decides the entire read load for the next interval.

Measured on a sentinel-backed `NewFailoverClusterClient` across three availability zones,
`GET`s per second on a five-replica set:

```
97.7   71.4   7.6   4.3   0.17        -> 590x spread
per-pod CPU: 38m 34m 39m 26m 27m      -> flat
```

CPU is flat, so the split follows the latency ranking rather than any real difference in
capacity. Locality itself works well — enabling `RouteByLatency` cut our cross-AZ transfer by
about 70% — but *within* a zone one replica of five was serving 0.17 reads/s. Egress showed
the same imbalance (4.81 vs 1.73 Gbit/s between the busiest and quietest), which is the part
that bites: the busiest node was at 77% of its instance's sustained network baseline while
others idled.

## Possible Solution

An opt-in tolerance: treat nodes within a configurable duration of the fastest as equal
candidates and round-robin between them using the existing `ShardPicker`. A node an
availability zone away is roughly 4x further off (~0.6ms vs ~0.15ms), so it stays outside any
sensible band and locality is preserved. A zero default keeps today's behaviour byte for byte.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a Redis Sentinel set with several replicas reachable at similar latency (in practice,
   two or more replicas in the same availability zone as the client).
2. Create a client with `RouteByLatency: true`:
   ```go
   rdb := redis.NewFailoverClusterClient(&redis.FailoverOptions{
       MasterName:     "mymaster",
       SentinelAddrs:  []string{":26379"},
       RouteByLatency: true,
   })
   ```
3. Issue read-only commands from several client processes.
4. Compare per-node `cmdstat_get` from `INFO commandstats`. The equally-close replicas do not
   share the load; one takes essentially all of it, and the winner changes when the latency
   estimate is refreshed.

## Context (Environment)

Sentinel-backed failover cluster client, three availability zones, five replicas per set,
go-redis v9.18.0 (behaviour is unchanged on current `master`).

replicas that are provisioned and paid for while serving almost no reads, and a hot node
approaching its network baseline. There is no way to express "these nodes are close enough,
spread across them" with the current options: `RouteRandomly` discards locality entirely, and

## Summary

We're observing a reproducible memory leak when using `go-redis` `ClusterClient` against an Azure Managed Redis Cluster (Enterprise, OSS Cluster Policy).

The service is eventually OOMKilled because heap memory grows continuously while connection pool size and goroutine count remain stable.

We upgraded from **v9.17.2** to **v9.21.0** expecting the fixes from #3678/#3680 and #3812/#3818 to resolve the issue, but the behavior is unchanged.

## Environment
- go-redis: v9.21.0 (also reproduced on v9.17.2)
- Redis: Azure Managed Redis Enterprise (OSS Cluster API), 2 shards
- Pool: PoolSize=50, MinIdleConns=2, MaxIdleConns=5, ConnMaxIdleTime=3m, ConnMaxLifetime=1h
- Workload: 30-50 concurrent goroutines/pod, bursty XReadGroup/XAutoClaim traffic, 3 pods, ~40 tenants/pod.

## Actual behavior
Heap grows from ~127MB to ~1.97GB in ~91 minutes until OOM.

PoolStats() shows TotalConns/IdleConns remain flat while StaleConns increases steadily (~4.8/sec).

pprof shows ~82% of retained heap in `bufio.NewReaderSize`/`bufio.NewWriterSize` allocated from `internal/pool.NewConnWithBufferSize`.

Allocation traces only show replacement/new idle connection paths.

- ~26k retained bufio.Reader
- ~26k retained bufio.Writer
- StaleConns=26,936

- Custom Hook retaining *pool.Conn
- StreamingCredentialsProvider listener leak (#3812)

## Mitigation
Increasing MaxIdleConns and ConnMaxIdleTime approximately halves both stale connection growth and heap growth, but memory still grows continuously.

## Question
Could this be another stale-connection retention path related to #3678/#3680 or #3812/#3818, or a separate leak where bufio.Reader/bufio.Writer remain reachable after stale connections are closed?

ClusterClient.SSubscribe silently re-subscribes to a random node after reconnect — PubSub.conn() ignores c.schannels

### Expected Behavior

A `*PubSub` created via `ClusterClient.SSubscribe` should reconnect to the
node owning the shard channel's hash slot after a connection failure, the
same way it does for the initial connection.

### Current Behavior

After any connection loss (server restart, transient network blip,
`CLIENT KILL`, idle timeout), the `PubSub` auto-reconnects to a **random
cluster node** and re-issues `SSUBSCRIBE` there. On any node other than the
slot owner, Redis replies `-MOVED`. The reply is never read (the `resubscribe`
path is write-only), so the failure is **silent**: the `PubSub` looks healthy,
`Ping` succeeds, `Receive`/`Channel()` keep returning, but no messages arrive
because the subscriber isn't on the shard the publishers reach.

On an N-node cluster the chance of landing on the wrong node is `(N-1)/N` per
reconnect. The only recovery is to close and recreate the `PubSub` (or restart
the process).

### Root Cause

[`pubsub.go:90`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/8cdff5946a35/pubsub.go#L90)
in `PubSub.conn()` builds the `channels` slice that's handed to the
`newConn` callback for node selection — but it only collects `c.channels`
(regular `SUBSCRIBE`), not `c.schannels` (sharded `SSUBSCRIBE`):

```go
channels := slices.Collect(maps.Keys(c.channels))
channels = append(channels, newChannels...)

cn, err := c.newConn(ctx, c.opt.Addr, channels)
```

For a `PubSub` that *only* has sharded subscriptions — the normal case for
`ClusterClient.SSubscribe` — `channels` is empty when reconnecting. The
`ClusterClient`'s `newConn` closure
([`osscluster.go:2152-2178`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/8cdff5946a35/osscluster.go#L2152-L2178))
then takes the `else` branch and picks a random node:

```go
if len(channels) > 0 {
    slot := hashtag.Slot(channels[0])
    ...
    node, err = c.slotMasterNode(ctx, slot)
    ...
} else {
    node, err = c.nodes.Random()       // ← reconnect lands here
    ...
}
```

`resubscribe()`
([`pubsub.go:127-128`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/8cdff5946a35/pubsub.go#L127-L128))
then writes `SSUBSCRIBE` over the new conn, but `_subscribe()` is
write-only and never reads the reply. The `-MOVED` from the wrong node is
either dropped, or eventually surfaces as an error from `ReceiveTimeout` —
but `isBadConn()`
([`error.go:204-210`](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/8cdff5946a35/error.go#L204-L210))
returns `false` for a `MOVED` that points at a *different* address, so it
doesn't trigger another reconnect.

The *initial* connection isn't affected, because `PubSub.subscribe()` passes

## Description

After upgrading from go-redis **v9.17.3** to **v9.18.0**, PubSub connections in a **TLS-only Redis cluster** (`--port 0 --tls-port 6379`) attempt to connect to port 0 instead of the correct TLS port 6379. Regular (non-PubSub) operations work correctly.

## Error

```
dial tcp 172.30.0.12:0: connect: connection refused
```

Logged as: `component=pubsub node_address=172.30.0.12:0`

## Environment

- Redis 7.4.8 cluster, 6 nodes (3 masters + 3 replicas)
- TLS-only mode: `--port 0 --tls-port 6379 --tls-cluster yes`
- go-redis v9.17.3 → v9.18.0

## Key observations

1. **CLUSTER SLOTS** returns the correct port 6379 for all nodes
2. **CLUSTER SHARDS** returns `tls-port: 6379` but no `port` field (expected for `--port 0` config)

5. Reverting to v9.17.3 fixes the issue completely

## Analysis

Compared the full diff between v9.17.3 and v9.18.0. The topology discovery via `ClusterSlots()` correctly returns port 6379. The issue appears to be in how PubSub connections are established in cluster mode.

- New `NodeAddress` field in `Options`

PubSub connects to port 0, which fails immediately.

Zombie connection in ConnPool.idleConns

Connections closed on +switch-master notification from Sentinel remains in ConnPool.idleConns forever

## Expected Behavior

Idle connections with state "CLOSED" should be cleaned up from ConnPool.idleConns and new connections should be reestablished.

## Current Behavior

Idle connections remains in ConnPool.idleConns forever.
Currently we use v9.17.2.

## Possible Solution

On v9.16.0 it works as expected.
First, on +switch-master event for every connection in pool p.closeConn(cn) is called. The difference between versions is a new line `cn.stateMachine.Transition(StateClosed)` in Conn.Close() method, which changes the state to "CLOSED".
Second, ConnPool.popIdle() behavior was changed.
In v9.16.0 the following code returns cn, which later is being tested in p.isHealthyConn(cn, now). As a result closed connection is being removed from pool.

```

		if cn.CompareAndSwapUsed(false, true) {
			if cn.IsUsable() {
				p.idleConnsLen.Add(-1)
				break
			}
			cn.SetUsed(false)
		}

```

In v9.17.2 the code above was replaced with the following:

```

		// Hot path optimization: try IDLE → IN_USE or CREATED → IN_USE transition
		// Using inline TryAcquire() method for better performance (avoids pointer dereference)
		if cn.TryAcquire() {
			// Successfully acquired the connection
			p.idleConnsLen.Add(-1)
			break
		}

```

cn.TryAcquire() will give True if and only if the stated is in "IDLE" or "CREATED". We have state "CLOSED" here, so as a result we have cn=nil. There are no remaining available connection in pool, so we go through the branch of code where for every upcoming commands a new connection is being created.

I believe we need to return closed cn from popIdle method to be cleared in isHealthyConn as before, or remove from pool here.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run redis in sentinel mode
2. Create a Failover Client with poolSize=1

```

		MasterName:      sentinelName,
		SentinelAddrs:   strings.Split(sentinels, ","),
		PoolSize:        1,
		DisableIdentity: true,
	})

```

3. Send at least one command to fill the pool
4. Trigger switch master
5. To easier catch the bug we can use multi-exec 

```
	
	set, err := client.Set(ctx, "testRadishKeyMulti2", "5", 0).Result()
	assert.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Equal(t, "OK", set)

	multi, err := client.Do(ctx, "MULTI").Result()

Memory leak: wrappedOnClose builds unbounded closure chain per initConn when using StreamingCredentialsProvider

## Versions

- **go-redis:** v9.18.0
- **Redis:** 6.x (reproduced with `redis:6` Docker image; bug is in go-redis, not Redis)

## What did you do?

Used `StreamingCredentialsProvider` with Azure EntraID token rotation (~45–90 min lifetime).
With `PoolSize=100`, the service OOM-killed every 18–22 hours in production.

## What did you expect?

Heap stays flat regardless of how many token rotations occur.

## What did you see instead?

Heap grows ~600 MB per rotation and kills the process.

Reproduction (PoolSize=10, 50 workers, 15s rotation interval):

```
heap=   2 MB  conns=10  stale=0      rotations=0
heap= 603 MB  conns=10  stale=8711   rotations=1
heap=1038 MB  conns=10  stale=15082  rotations=2
heap=3343 MB  conns=10  stale=47059  rotations=11   (3 minutes)
```

## Root cause

In `redis.go:486`, inside `initConn`:

```go
c.onClose = c.wrappedOnClose(unsubscribeFromCredentialsProvider)  // line 486 — BUG
cn.SetOnClose(unsubscribeFromCredentialsProvider)                  // line 487 — correct
```

`wrappedOnClose` captures the current `c.onClose` in a new closure and returns a wrapper
that calls both. Called on every `initConn`, this builds an unbounded linked list on the
**shared `baseClient`**:

```
initConn #1: c.onClose = wrap(unsub_1, nil)
initConn #2: c.onClose = wrap(unsub_2, wrap(unsub_1, nil))
initConn #3: c.onClose = wrap(unsub_3, wrap(unsub_2, wrap(unsub_1, nil)))
...
initConn #N: chain of N closures, each retaining a dead *pool.Conn (~70 KB TLS buffers)
```

This chain lives on the shared `baseClient` and is only walked at `Close()` — never trimmed
during normal operation. The leak is amplified by `ReAuthPoolHook`: during a token rotation
the hook rejects all pooled connections simultaneously, firing a storm of
`queuedNewConn → initConn` calls that rapidly extends the chain.

`cn.SetOnClose` on line 487 already correctly handles per-connection unsubscription when
individual connections close. Line 486 is redundant and harmful.

## Fix

```diff
-        c.onClose = c.wrappedOnClose(unsubscribeFromCredentialsProvider)
         cn.SetOnClose(unsubscribeFromCredentialsProvider)
```

With the fix applied, heap stays flat at ~3 MB for the full 3-minute run.

## Minimal reproduction

```bash
docker run --rm -p 6399:6379 redis:6 redis-server --requirepass test-token
go run main.go
```

Self-contained ~130-line reproduction: https://gist.github.com/fxsml/0191f9a91b62078ddecf84cd94160e9f

- #3542 — unexpected `used` connection count spike with `StreamingCredentialsProvider` (same `ReAuthPoolHook` path)
- #3582 — hook rejection errors after v9.16 upgrade (same path)

Vector Set commands don't handle RESP2 responses.

## Expected Behavior

`VectorScoreSliceCmd` (used by `VSimWithScores`, `VSimWithArgsWithScores`, `VLinksWithScores`) should correctly parse replies from both RESP2 and RESP3 connections.

## Current Behavior

`VectorScoreSliceCmd.readReply` calls `rd.ReadMapLen()` directly without first checking the reply type via `PeekReplyType()`. This means it only works with RESP3 (map) responses and will fail on RESP2 connections, which return flat arrays.

## Possible Solution

Update `VectorScoreSliceCmd.readReply` to peek the reply type and handle both RESP2 (flat array of `[name, score, name, score, ...]`) and RESP3 (map of `name -> score`) formats, similar to how the new `VectorAttribSliceCmd` and `VectorScoreAttribSliceCmd` in #3753 already handle both protocols.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Connect to Redis 8.x using RESP2 (default protocol)
2. Create a vector set and add elements
3. Call `VSimWithScores` or `VLinksWithScores`
4. Observe a parse error from `ReadMapLen` failing on an array reply

## Context (Environment)

Any RESP2 connection to Redis 8.x+ with vector set commands.

## Detailed Description

The `VectorScoreSliceCmd.readReply` in `command.go` assumes the reply is always a RESP3 map. On RESP2 connections, Redis returns a flat array (`[name1, score1, name2, score2, ...]`), which causes `ReadMapLen` to fail. This affects all commands returning `*VectorScoreSliceCmd`: `VSimWithScores`, `VSimWithArgsWithScores`, and `VLinksWithScores`.

## Possible Implementation

Add a `PeekReplyType()` check at the top of `readReply`. If the type is `proto.RespMap`, use the current map-based parsing. If it's an array, read the array length, verify it's a multiple of 2, and parse `[name, score]` pairs sequentially.

FailoverClient (with ReplicaOnly) times out on unavailable Sentinel and terminates search for a live one.

## Expected Behavior

FailoverClient successfully finds an available Sentinel and establishes a connection.

## Current Behavior

FailoverClient.replicaAddrs terminates immediately if it tries to connect to a Sentinel that is network-unavailable.
(see Detailed Description)

## Possible Solution

Need to check outer context expiration instead of checking if the returned error matches context.DeadlineExceeded.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run several Redis-server+Sentinel instances locally (6379+26379 <- leader, 6380+26380, 6381+26381)
2. Simulate network timeout for connection to one of them (block in firewall via packet drop, not reject)
   blocking via pfctl (reproducing on mac os x)
   ```
   block drop in proto tcp from any to any port = 6381
   block drop in proto tcp from any to any port = 26381
   ```
3. Create FailoverClient and execute a command (Ping) (check [main_sentinel.go](https://gist.github.com/perekalov/8f710337a3dd6ba8873886c7198c610a))
4. During the first command, discovery occurs, and if [shuffle](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/sentinel.go#L407) places the problematic sentinel first, the connection establishment will timeout and the command may fail with an error without trying to connect to other live Sentinels.

Log file containing multiple executions (`main_sentinel.log`) is attached. In certain cases, the connection can still be established (see Detailed Description).

## Detailed Description

Under the hood, the driver creates a network connection via `net.Dialer`.
The `DialContext` method in case of network timeout can return an error that can be interpreted as `context.DeadlineExceeded`: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/51428
For example, this happens when the Timeout expires during connection (this parameter is [set](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/sentinel.go#L467) by go-redis).

That is, `Dialer.DialContext` can return an error (comparable to `context.DeadlineExceeded`), not because the context passed from outside has expired, but due to an internal connection timeout.
The go-redis code, as far as I can see, expects that the `context.DeadlineExceeded` error means the expiration of the context passed from outside.

Thus `sentinelFailover.replicaAddrs` fails with `context.DeadlineExceeded` error when encountering an unavailable Sentinel, even if the context passed to the command has no timeout set.
This breaks the failover mechanism's core purpose of finding available sentinels.

Check [main_deal.go](https://gist.github.com/perekalov/bc90689409952dcc7af702415ee5af9e) for reproduction. Again, packet drop needs to be configured on port 26381.
A log file from one of the runs is attached too (`main_deal.log`). Interestingly, _sometimes_ the function doesn't wrap `i/o timeout` in `context.DeadlineExceeded`, and `replicaAddrs` proceeds to check the next Sentinel and ultimately finds a live one.
But according to the mentioned change in the standard library code, we should assume that it should behave exactly this way.

Proposal: Align context handling for connection creation with database/sql and net/http

### Description

In high-concurrency scenarios where the connection pool is exhausted, the `go-redis` library currently uses the incoming request's context (`reqCtx`) for the entire connection creation process (dialing, TLS handshake, AUTH, etc.) in `ConnPool.Get`. This creates a critical issue that is at odds with the established best practices implemented in the Go standard library.

If the request times out while the connection is being established, the dialing operation is canceled. This often happens even if the connection is milliseconds away from completion, leading to several detrimental effects that are exacerbated by certain common conditions:

**Three key factors compound this problem:**

1. **PoolTimeout Compression:** The configured `PoolTimeout` period is consumed while waiting for an available connection. By the time a new connection creation is initiated, a significant portion of the request's original timeout budget may already be exhausted, leaving an insufficient time window for the dialing operation to complete successfully. This makes connection establishment far more likely to fail.
2. **Asymmetric Timeout Configurations:** For latency-sensitive services, the timeout on the request context (dictated by upstream service level objectives) is often significantly shorter than a reasonable `DialTimeout` (which must account for network latency and TCP/TLS handshakes). This mismatch means the request is likely to time out well before the underlying dial operation has had a fair chance to succeed.
3. **Propagated Context Timeout Decay:** In distributed systems, the timeout on a request's context is typically set by the initial upstream client and decays as it propagates through the service chain. By the time it reaches a downstream service like Redis, the remaining time is frequently very short—often just milliseconds. This leaves virtually no time for a new connection to be established from scratch, making failures almost certain under pool contention.
    

**These factors lead directly to the following negative outcomes:**

1.  **Unnecessary connection establishment failures:** Perfectly good connections are aborted due to brief client-side timeouts.
2.  **Connection pool starvation:** A storm of timed-out requests can prevent the pool from ever being refilled, causing a cascade of failures for subsequent requests.
3.  **Diagnostic ambiguity and operational overhead:** It becomes extremely difficult to distinguish between genuine server-side/network connectivity issues and client-side timeout pressure. Observing a high rate of connection timeouts could indicate a problem with the Redis server, or it could simply be a symptom of the client's own aggressive timeouts cancelling viable connections. This ambiguity makes alerting, debugging, and root cause analysis significantly more complex and time-consuming.
4.  **Resource waste:** Server-side resources (TCP slots, CPU for TLS handshakes) are used without any benefit.

### Prior Art in Go Stdlib and the Robust Solution

This is a well-understood problem in connection pool design. The Go standard library's `database/sql` and `net/http` packages have already implemented robust solutions to prevent request timeouts from destabilizing the connection pool.

**1. database/sql.DB**
The `sql.DB` pool decouples connection creation from request lifecycles. It uses a long-lived, dedicated goroutine (`connectionOpener`) to serialize connection creation. Crucially, **it uses a background context for the connection establishment itself**.
*   **Source Code Reference:**
    *   The `connectionOpener` goroutine: [`sql.OpenDB`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7bba745820b771307593b7278ce17464eeda2f3d/src/database/sql/sql.go#L841)
    *   The `openNewConnection` method which uses the opener's context: [`(*DB).openNewConnection`](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/7bba745820b771307593b7278ce174

Why does go-redis allow cluster mode cross-shard transactions and pipelines?

Cross-shard/cross-slot batch operations in cluster mode-enabled clusters, like transactions and pipelines, are not supported in a Redis cluster, by specification.

* There is no server-side primitive that enables cross-shard transactional atomicity.
* A single pipeline cannot physically be applied to multiple targets, since it occurs over a single physical connection.

OK
127.0.0.1:7002> set b bbbbb

OK

NewClient panics when given nil Options - add nil parameter check

## Expected Behavior

`_ = redis.NewClient(nil)`

When `opt` parameter is `nil`, `NewClient` should handle it gracefully (e.g., use default configuration or return an error) instead of causing a panic.

## Current Behavior

If `opt` is `nil`, calling `opt.init()` triggers a **nil pointer dereference panic**, leading to program crash.

## Possible Solution

Add a nil check for `opt` parameter and initialize it with default values when it's `nil`:

```go
func NewClient(opt *Options) *Client {
	if opt == nil {
		opt = &Options{} // Use default configuration or actively panic
	}
	// ...
}
```

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a `nil` `*Options` instance: `var opt *redis.Options`
2. Call `redis.NewClient(opt)`  
3. The program panics with error: `panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`

## Context (Environment)

Affects developers using the Go-Redis client library. This issue can lead to unexpected application crashes when `NewClient` is called with an uninitialized `Options` pointer.

## Detailed Description

The `NewClient` method does not validate the `opt` parameter for `nil` before calling `opt.init()`. When `opt` is `nil`, this results in a critical runtime panic. This violates defensive programming principles and exposes the library to misuse by clients that might pass invalid configurations.

## Possible Implementation

1. Add a nil check at the beginning of `NewClient`:
```
func NewClient(opt *Options) *Client {
	if opt == nil {
		opt = &Options{} // Initialize with default values
	}
	opt.init() 
	// ... rest of the implementation
}
```
2. Update documentation to clarify that `opt` can be `nil` (with defaults) or explicitly initialized.

`RouteByLatency` leads to significant ping load when all servers of a shard are failed

When the OSS ClusterClient uses the `RouteByLatency` option and a shard is completely down, it will ping every server in the cluster 10 times as much as every 200ms. This can lead to millions of pings per second for production Redis clusters with a large number of clients.

## Expected Behavior
`RouteByLatency` should limit pings to servers only when latency to servers are expected to have change or when a server does not yet have a latency measurement.

## Current Behavior

`RouteByLatency` can ping as much as up to 10 times to every server every 200 ms, and will ping at this frequency when all servers of a shard are marked as failing. This happens for every cluster client.

## Possible Solution
The behavior to reload the state when there are failovers/topology changes is advantageous as we want the cluster client to have the latest cluster state; this seems to be the only way a server can go from a "failing" state back to a healthy state. Often servers that were healthy before and after the state refresh and were present in both will not have changes in their latency, but servers that may be recovering from failures may be moved in a cloud service provider and have different latencies.

We can consider splitting the conditions for probing latencies of servers - on topology changes/failovers, probe the latency of servers that are new or were previously failed in the state. Otherwise, probe the latency of servers only if the previous latency measurement is sufficiently old (> 10s).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a OSS Redis cluster with 3 shards and no read replicas. 
2. Create a test client that issues requests to every shard, [example test client gist](https://gist.github.com/justinmir/fcf949544d7f11f43d56ab0121449b36).
3. Shut down redis on a single server in the 3 server cluster - failing one third of the slots.
4. Observe the ping rate to the redis cluster.

Use of `RouteByLatency` introduces additional risk to production clusters, it can limit availability of requests
to all shards when a single shard fails.

In a production incident, this occurred in an 80 node (40 shard) cluster with hundreds of thousands of client connections.

## Detailed Description

**How/When does go-redis ping servers to determine latency**
`RouteByLatency` will issue pings to redis servers to determine their latency. It does this by issuing 10 pings to every
server in the cluster.

It does this under several conditions:
1. A new OSS cluster client is created.
2. A client receives an unexpected `READONLY` reply from a redis client ([link](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L946))
3. **A client receives a `MOVED` reply from a redis client ([link](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L964))**
4. Roughly every 10 seconds, anytime the cluster state is required to process a command ([link](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L825)).

Each of these places calls `LazyReload` which limits reloading to [once every 200ms](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L814).

Anytime a reload happens, we load the state and perform `GC` one minute after loading the state. This `GC` operation will issue a call to update the latencies to each of the servers. ([Call to GC](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L656), [call to update server latency](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/master/osscluster.go#L491)).

Connection health checks completely ineffective for TLS connections

This is to report a bug in the health check logic for TLS connections. Specifically, in the `connCheck` function in the `internal/pool/conn_check.go` file [here](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/f752b9a9d5cc158381c2ffe5b13c531037426b39/internal/pool/conn_check.go#L19).  It leads to unintentional exhaustions of retry count and ultimately command failures, in the presence of server-side disconnections.

`go-redis` with non-TLS does not have this problem. 

## Expected Behavior

The intended use case of connection health check, when [picking connections from pool, a health check is made](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/f752b9a9d5cc158381c2ffe5b13c531037426b39/internal/pool/pool.go#L259-L299). Bad connections are thrown away immediately. The code keeps picking until a good connection is found. If all pooled connections are bad, a new connection is made. Throwing away a bad connection does not consume retry count. Only when a error happened when using a picked connection to send a command, that error would [consume a retry count to be retried](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/f752b9a9d5cc158381c2ffe5b13c531037426b39/redis.go#L400-L446).

## Current Behavior

The specific bug is, when using TLS, the input argument of the `connCheck` [function](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/f752b9a9d5cc158381c2ffe5b13c531037426b39/internal/pool/conn_check.go#L19) is of `tls.Conn` type. `tls.Conn` [type](https://pkg.go.dev/crypto/tls#Conn) does not implement the `syscall.Conn` [interface](https://pkg.go.dev/syscall#Conn). As result, the type conversion [here](https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/f752b9a9d5cc158381c2ffe5b13c531037426b39/internal/pool/conn_check.go#L19) always returns `ok` being `false` therefore bypassing connection health check entirely for TLS connections. Bad connections in the connection pool are used to send commands, resulting in errors. Every bad connection consumes a retry count.

### Description
Introduce new commands that enable setting expiration times for individual fields within a hash. These commands will mirror existing Redis commands for setting key expiration but will be adapted for hash fields.

### Proposed Commands
1. **HEXPIRE**: Set TTL in seconds for specified fields within a hash.
2. **HPEXPIRE**: Set TTL in milliseconds for specified fields within a hash.
3. **HEXPIREAT**: Set expiration time as a UNIX timestamp in seconds for specified fields.
4. **HPEXPIREAT**: Set expiration time as a UNIX timestamp in milliseconds for specified fields.
5. **HPERSIST**: Remove expiration time from specified fields.
6. **HEXPIRETIME**: Retrieve the expiration time in seconds for specified fields.
7. **HPEXPIRETIME**: Retrieve the expiration time in milliseconds for specified fields.
8. **HTTL**: Retrieve the TTL in seconds for specified fields.
9. **HPTTL**: Retrieve the TTL in milliseconds for specified fields.

Feedback on the implementations is highly welcome. Please share any concerns or additional features that should be considered.

[BUGS] data race in connection pool management

There is a data race issue in this `newConn` function. This function is not thread-safe. https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2512123b7686dca1f7f0208eaada6cdf3ef0189c/internal/pool/pool.go#L166-L194

There's a shared variable `p.poolSize`.

There is a read access to `p.poolSize` on line 171: https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2512123b7686dca1f7f0208eaada6cdf3ef0189c/internal/pool/pool.go#L171

There is a write access to `p.poolSize` on line 189: https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2512123b7686dca1f7f0208eaada6cdf3ef0189c/internal/pool/pool.go#L189

While the mutex enforced on line 180 can only make writes mutually exclusive: https://github.com/redis/go-redis/blob/2512123b7686dca1f7f0208eaada6cdf3ef0189c/internal/pool/pool.go#L180-L181

In such a situation, there's a data race:

goroutine #1 is reading `p.poolSize` (on line 171, it does not need to acquire the mutex lock)

goroutine #2 is writing to `p.poolSize` (on line 189, it needs to acquire the mutex lock in order to write)

This shared variable `p.poolSize` is concurrently accessed by two goroutines, one read and one write, resulting in a data race issue

## Expected Behavior

There should not be a data race issue when the `newConn` function is called

## Current Behavior

There is a data race issue

## Possible Solution

There is a data race because the mutex does not protect the full scope of the critical section, but only part of it. We should run `p.connsMu.Lock()` and `defer p.connsMu.Unlock()` earlier than it is, or use a `RLock` to protect read to the shared variable `p.poolSize` while `RWLock` to protect write

SCAN fails to parse cursor value out of int64 range

SCAN cursor is an `unsigned 64 bit number` in Redis protocol. It's defined at https://redis.io/commands/scan as:

```
SCAN, SSCAN, HSCAN and ZSCAN return a two elements multi-bulk reply, 
where the first element is a string representing an unsigned 64 bit number (the cursor)...
```
But the cursor is read as an `int64` at https://github.com/go-redis/redis/blob/31f6ce03990aac1d06f366bb998ffef9713969e5/command.go#L2697

which fails to parse result if the cursor value is out of `int64` range, like;

```
strconv.ParseInt: parsing "14430143861864273311": value out of range
```

In v8, it was being read as `uint`: https://github.com/go-redis/redis/blob/6c688c7e9f6276867db4d09b1c48babb45cf2a93/internal/proto/reader.go#L216-L225

No way to use ScanIterator concurrently - consider dropping mutex or changing signature

## Expected Behavior

`ScanIterator` doc says it's safe for concurrent use.

## Current Behavior

If one goroutine calls `Next()` then it cannot call `Val()` safely because another goroutine might have called `Next()` at that moment, moving to the next value. In that case a value will be missed, obviously leading to problems.

## Possible Solution

Either remove mutex and doc, stating it's safe for concurrent use OR change the interface, allowing for safe concurrent iteration.

I think it'd be much better to just remove the mutex and let the called wrap it in a mutex if they need to. Even if `NextVal() (string, error)` is introduced, there is no safe way to e.g. iterate over a key-value map, such as `HScan` result. Perhaps `NextPair() (string, string, error)` can be introduced? Or maybe a new `PairIterator`? That'd be useful in any case, but I think mutex should be removed regardless - most users don't need to pay the lock/unlock cost.

I think it's a great time to make this breaking change (well, anyone who is using the current API concurrently is already broken) before v9 is released.

undefined: otel.Meter or cannot find package "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/api/trace"

To fix `cannot find package "go.opentelemetry.io/otel/api/trace"` or `undefined: otel.Meter`:

1. Make sure to initialize a [Go module](https://blog.golang.org/using-go-modules): `go mod init github.com/my/repo`

2. Make sure to use correct import path with *v8* in the end: `go get github.com/go-redis/redis/v8`

For example:

```bash
mkdir /tmp/redis-test
cd /tmp/redis-test
go mod init redis-test
go get github.com/go-redis/redis/v8
```

## The root cause

The error is not caused by OpenTelemetry. OpenTelemetry is just the first module Go tries to install. And the error will not go away until you start using [Go modules](https://blog.golang.org/using-go-modules) properly.

The presence of **$GOROOT** or **$GOPATH** in error messages indicates that you are NOT using Go modules.

I believe `func (c *clusterStateHolder) LazyReload(ctx context.Context)` is being called sometimes with the same context as the main command (a simple get in this example). By the time the reload completes the context used for the main command may have been cancelled.

## Expected Behavior

4. Check the lazy reload failed.

I am passing the http.Request.Context() to the redis command. I believe this context gets cancelled at the end of the http request.

Race condition in context cancellation for cluster commands

When updating to the latest go-redis driver, we hit a problem in our CI test suite where it showed up with a data race. We run our CI suite with the race detector enabled to catch problems. It triggered after updating the go-redis driver (v8.0.0-beta.7 to v8.4.0). It looks like it is a race bug inside the Redis driver and not in our code. We also were able to reproduce the race with a test script independent from our project.

## Expected Behavior

```go
func TestXReadRace(t *testing.T) {
	client := redis.NewIntegrationRedis(t)
	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())

	for i := 0; i < 100; i++ {
		stream := fmt.Sprintf("foo.test.%d", i)
		go func() {
			_, err := client.XRead(ctx, &goredis.XReadArgs{
				Streams: []string{stream, "$"},
				Block:   1 * time.Second,
			}).Result()
			if err != context.Canceled {
				panic(err)
			}
		}()
	}

	time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond)
	cancel()
}
```

We'd expect that this operation wouldn't trigger the race detector, but that here `err` returned from `XRead` has the message that the context was cancelled.

	if retry < 0 {

Particular configuration can cause mismatched responses

Using the `ClusterClient` with `ReadOnly` set and `MaxRetries` > 0 can lead to serious bugged client state.

In short, if a timeout or other retryable error occurs, the connection can buffer responses incorrectly, so you can get into a state where your code is:
```
msg, err := client.Echo("message").Result()
log.Println("msg:", msg) // should print "msg: message"
log.Println("err:", err) // should print: "err: <nil>"
```
 can in fact print "msg: OK" and others.

This can lead to states where the client is unknowingly returning totally incorrect, but valid-looking responses with no error:

```
Within Redis server: <AAAA: "hello", BBBB: "world">
msg, err = client.Get("AAAA").Result() // "OK", <nil>
msg, err = client.Get("BBBB").Result() // "hello", <nil>
```

I've created https://github.com/patrickwhite256/goredis-bug-demo which contains a fake redis "server" and a script that can trip the bug. Because it's not a real Redis server, it's not proof positive of the bug, so I have also included a detailed explanation of what exactly needs to happen to trip the bug all the way down the stack.

I've opened #1112 to address this.
